title: Elric and the Lost Sunstone
markdown:
In the heart of Aethelgard, where paths climbed the peaks like silver ribbon, lived Elric, an elf whose ears were a little too generous for his head and whose moss-green eyes missed very little: a hawk’s flicker, lichen’s handwriting on stone. He was mountain-bred and carried a quiet that his brothers, who could charm stars into conversation, tended to talk over.

One sunny morning he was given the mushroom stall at Oakhaven market. He arranged the caps, still dewed, and watched the town go past. The work had the pace of moss. He wanted a deed that echoed. He wanted, less usefully, to prove that quiet was not the same as small.

Rivulet, his pine marten, sat on a crate. Fur like oak bark, motions like punctuation. They shared a language of whisker and tail.

To pass the hour Elric took a smooth stone from his pocket and tried a small charm — the sort that asked ordinary objects to help, a dropped spoon, a rolled button. His siblings called it lesser magic. He chose an old broom against the stall. “A wiggle,” he whispered, and used the old words.

The air shimmered, then startled. The broom jerked upright, bristles twitching, a puff of dust like a sneeze. Not a wiggle. It pointed its head at a loose flagstone and tapped: thud, thud, thud.

Elric’s shyness stepped aside for curiosity. “What is it?” Rivulet was already sniffing. Together they eased the stone. In the cool earth lay a scroll no bigger than a thumb. Wind, helpful for once, tipped it into Elric’s palm.

Faded ink, almost glowing: The Sunstone is lost, a shadow falls. Seek the Librarian’s Lair ere the festival calls.

The Sunstone was the Harvest Festival’s heart, lit at dusk to keep autumn from the square. Without it the evening would be only evening. Elric’s pulse found a faster job. A real errand. Also the old fear: trying in public and being seen to fail. His palms went damp.

Rivulet nudged his hand, chirped a short confident run of notes, tail on purpose. Elric nodded. One step. Then another.

They left the busy square by a path less travelled, one that climbed into rockier slopes where the air remembered it had a job. Pine and damp earth filled the lungs. Old whispers — the kind mountain folk pass down when they are not teasing anyone about lesser magic — pointed them toward a hidden mouth in the cliff, almost lost under a curtain of ivy like green lace. Elric took a breath that had more courage in it than volume, and pushed through the rustle.

The cave was still and smelled of paper and a memory of lavender. Not a dungeon: a room carved into shelves, scrolls in faded ribbon, books with patterned hides, parchment that rustled as if it had opinions. On a cushion in the centre sat a cat the colour of a night that had decided to stay. Emerald eyes took the light from above and kept it.

“Greetings, seekers.” A purr like sun-warmed stone. “I am Shadow. You want the Sunstone.”

Elric explained, words arriving faster than dignity. Shadow’s tail measured the time. “Not stolen. Hidden. My predecessor — kind, forgetful — feared a hard season and put it away. His memory went like mist. He did not write the where.”

No villain, then. A gap in a list. Shadow offered a riddle, leaves in the voice:

“I hold the sun, yet cast no shade.
Within a tale, my light is laid.
Where mountain roots reach deep and old,
My gleam awaits, a story told.”

Elric thought of his brothers’ pronouncements, then of the small things he actually saw. “A tale…” Rivulet darted to a stack of scrolls, sniffed, dismissed them with a chirp, and pointed his chin at a thick book on a high shelf. Dark hide, title gone, cover drawn with alpine plants and the kind of roots that mean business.

“Mountain roots.” Elric’s eyes widened. “A plant book. An old one.” He climbed a ledge that had been waiting, fingers on the rough cover, and eased the volume down. In a hollow cut through the pages the Sunstone pulsed, gold and afternoon-warm. The air around it hummed as if it had been holding a note.

Violet and rose were already at the cave mouth. They ran the path toward Oakhaven. Festival clatter mixed with worried voices. Elric held the gem; its glow made a small argument against the dusk.

He reached the square as the Elder — a gnome with a beard like spun silver — drew breath to cancel the lighting. Gasps. Elric stepped forward, stone high. “I found it.” The voice surprised him by carrying. Relief went through the crowd like weather changing its mind. The Elder took the Sunstone; warmth unrolled; the gem flared and painted the square gold enough to make evening look hired.

Applause arrived in a wave. Elric’s family, who had been wearing surprise, adjusted it toward respect. He had not woven the stars. He had looked under a flagstone and read a cover.

Later, festival lamps like fallen stars and music finding the lanes, Elric sat with Rivulet by the hearth in their mountain home. A quiet that was not the market’s boredom settled in. The broom, back at the stall, was only a broom again, leaning as if it had never pointed at a mystery. He turned the empty pocket that had held the scroll. His brothers, at the festival, had clapped like everyone else; tomorrow they would weave stars again, and he would notice lichen. That seemed a fair division. He did not ask the trees to remember. Rivulet cleaned a paw and looked, as usual, as if the next ordinary object was already considering a career.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
